lessons.title: Review — one question, three answers
lessons.gloss: review — one question, asked of every past sentence, and the three answers it can have

needs: your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to all of it now and come back to the parts that need looking at once you have stopped.

segments.text: Nothing new. Before the table: do the two past tenses differ in when?
Three chapters, one question, three ways it gets answered.

utterances: what you are doing: reporting an event, with edges. tense: preterite. example: hablé — I spoke.
what you are doing: setting a scene, no edges. tense: imperfect. example: hablaba — I was speaking.
what you are doing: naming a state. tense: imperfect. example: tenía — I had.
what you are doing: naming the moment a state began. tense: preterite. example: tuve — I got.

segments.text: Rows one and two are the same event seen from two places. Rows three and four are not: there the tense changes what happened.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the question to actually ask

segments.text: Not "which tense is this?" — that has no answer without you.
Am I telling you what happened, or what things were like?
What happened has edges: preterite. What things were like does not: imperfect. A story is mostly the second with the first dropped into it, which is what cuando let you build:

And when the verb names a state rather than an action, the same question still works — you are simply more likely to be describing what things were like, so the imperfect is the ordinary case and the preterite is the special one.

There is no list to memorise here, and that is deliberate. Lists of "preterite trigger words" exist in most courses and they fail exactly where the choice is interesting, because the same word can sit in either sentence. The question does not fail, because the question is the thing the language is actually asking.

segments.instruction: "hablé / hablaba", then "tenía / tuve", and name the difference in each pair

segments.text: Until the question arrives before the verb does.

segments.prompt: State the one question that chooses the tense.
acceptedResponses: am i saying what happened or what things were like
what happened versus what things were like

feedback.incorrect: Am I telling what happened, or what things were like?

segments.prompt: In estudiaba cuando hablo Ana, which verb is the scene?

feedback.correct: And hablo is what walked into it.
feedback.incorrect: Estudiaba — the imperfect sets the room.

segments.prompt: Which two rows of the table are NOT the same event seen twice?
acceptedResponses: the state rows, tenia and tuve

feedback.correct: There the tense changes what happened, not just the view.
feedback.incorrect: The state rows: tenia is having, tuve is getting.

segments.text: The one question? (What happened, or what things were like?) Which pair changes meaning rather than viewpoint? (Tenía and tuve.) Next: a whole small story, which is what all of this was for.
